architecture.approach: Retroactive plan of the implemented design. A TimeEntry document is the single record of logged work; a partial unique index makes at most one running timer per user and workspace possible, so the timer does not need a lock or a separate store. Task-scoped routes live on the tasks router (/tasks/:id/time, /tasks/:id/timer/start|stop) and the workspace-wide reads on a small time router (/time, /time/running, /time/export.csv). All arithmetic is pure and lives in server/src/utils/timeTracking.ts, so the controllers only validate, query and serialise. The client keeps one timer store shared by the header pill and the task dialog, re-reads entries when the time-changed event fires, and derives the weekly grid from the entries with the pure helpers in features/time/lib.

dataModel.flowDescription: Logging by hand creates a stopped entry with whole minutes and resynchronises the task's loggedMinutes. Starting a timer looks for the caller's running entry in that workspace: if it points at the same task the entry is returned as is, otherwise it is stopped (capped at a day, at least one minute) and logged before a new running entry is created, which the partial unique index guarantees can only be one per user and workspace. Stopping a timer ends it, recomputes the task total and records an audit entry with the duration. Reads take two shapes: the task view returns the estimate, the total, the caller's running entry and up to 500 recent entries, while the timesheet filters stopped entries by date range, user and project and returns totals by user, day and task - or the same rows as CSV for the export.

securityConsiderations.description: Workspace isolation (CON-106): every TimeEntry read and write carries workspace: req.workspace._id, the task is resolved with the same workspace id, and the project filter is turned into the ids of that project's tasks inside the workspace, so a filter can never reach another workspace's rows.

Permissions run before the handler (CON-512) while the entry-level rule stays in the controller (CON-105): tasks:read for reads, tasks:write for logging, timers and deletion, and inside deleteTimeEntry (and the timesheet's user filter) the caller must be the author or hold settings:manage, otherwise 403.

Input validation (CON-515, CON-516): validateTimeEntry caps minutes at 1440 and the note at 200 characters and requires either minutes or both timestamps; range bounds are parsed by parseRangeBound, which rejects anything that is not a day key or a valid ISO instant, and ids are cast before use.

The CSV export neutralises spreadsheet formula injection: csvCell prefixes an apostrophe to any value starting with =, +, -, @, tab or carriage return, and quotes every field with inner quotes doubled.

performanceConsiderations.strategy: The task total is computed with a single aggregate over stopped entries instead of a document per entry, project keys are fetched once per response with one query over the distinct project names, and the timesheet pins the project filter to a task id list only when that filter is used.
Both reads are bounded: the task view selects the last 500 entries and the timesheet loads limit + 1 rows to detect truncation, so a large history cannot produce an unbounded response.

risks.description: loggedMinutes on the task is a denormalised total that can go stale if entries are changed outside the controller.
risks.mitigation: Every mutating path calls syncLogged, which recomputes the total from the entries and returns it in the response.

risks.description: A forgotten timer keeps running while the browser is closed.
risks.mitigation: timerEnd caps an entry at one day, the running timer is visible in the header wherever the user navigates, and starting another timer stops the previous one.

risks.description: Server totals group by UTC day while the weekly grid groups by the viewer's local day, so a late-evening entry can sit under a different day in the two views.
risks.mitigation: The grid uses the local calendar day of the entry (localDayKey) and the week range is built from local week boundaries, so the entries are always inside the requested window; the difference is documented as an assumption in the spec.
